extracted.intended_audience: researchers, clinicians and instrument developers selecting or validating resilience questionnaires; psychometricians and public-health researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic evaluation of resilience measurement instruments focusing on their psychometric properties and suitability for different populations and uses (clinical, research, cross-cultural).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which items reflect the construct of resilience (including multi-level facets: individual, family, community and culture) and whether items were developed from the literature and/or involved the target population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the dimensions are outlined and items map to them; check if target population/focus groups were involved in item development (the CYRM involved youths in 9 countries); note lack of transparency about item lists and wording as a weakness. Consider cultural/contextual relevance and whether the measure minimises situational effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which items within a scale/subscale are correlated, typically reported using Cronbach's alpha.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess whether sub-scales are sufficiently correlated to indicate they measure the same construct; consider reporting of alphas for subscales and overall scale. Internal consistency was the most commonly reported property in applied studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the measure correlates appropriately with a gold standard or external criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report how the instrument relates to recognized criterion measures when available; Table 4 includes 'Criterion Validity' as a distinct quality domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the measure behaves as expected according to theoretical predictions (e.g., factor structure, convergent/divergent validity, longitudinal evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for theoretical grounding (some measures like ER-89 and Psychological Resilience present strong theory), empirical tests (factor analyses, correlations with related constructs), and longitudinal evidence identifying features of resilient people. Lack of construct validity was noted for several measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility — agreement (absolute measurement error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information on agreement (absolute measurement error) between repeated measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report indices of agreement; the review found information on agreement was absent in all papers. Agreement is distinct from reliability and necessary to judge measurement error versus true change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility — reliability (test–retest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stability of scores over time when no real change is expected, typically reported as test–retest correlations or ICCs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report type of reliability analysis, ICC type, sample size and time interval. Aim for test–retest coefficients generally >0.70 for subscales; note small sample sizes (e.g., ICC for CD-RISC reported with n=24) and unspecified procedures reduce confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability of the instrument to detect clinically or practically important change over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include longitudinal pre–post evaluations and comparisons between responders and non-responders (the CD-RISC was the only measure examined for change in one trial). Define a Minimal Important Change (MIC) and report whether score changes correspond to clinical improvement; provide effect sizes and sufficient data to compute them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floor and ceiling effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which a large proportion of respondents obtain the lowest or highest possible scores, limiting ability to detect change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the presence/extent of floor/ceiling effects; the review found these were not reported for any measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretability
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaningfulness of scores — availability of subgroup means/SDs, cut-offs, categories and information on what constitutes clinically meaningful change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide norms, subgroup analyses and guidance on categorical interpretation (e.g., RS provides low/medium/high ranges). Define MIC and give data (means, SDs, sample sizes) to allow sample-size calculations for trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical rationale / conceptual adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity and appropriateness of the underlying definition of resilience and whether the measure reflects that conceptualisation (e.g., process vs. outcome, multi-level ecological models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures should align with a clear conceptual definition (the review favours a multi-level ecological perspective). Evaluate whether items operationalise the intended concept (assets/resources vs. bouncing back) and whether theoretical literature was used to justify item selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item development and selection transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentation of how items were generated, refined and selected (e.g., literature sources, qualitative interviews, verbatim items, pilot testing, data-reduction methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice includes presenting the initial item pool, describing wording choices and reporting piloting/feedback. The absence of full item lists or unclear data-reduction methods (noted for several measures) weakens confidence in content coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural appropriateness and cross‑national validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the instrument is meaningful and valid across different cultural contexts and that cross-cultural development/adaptation was performed appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider emic perspectives, involvement of local target groups, and multi-country development (e.g., CYRM developed in 11 countries). Recognise that key factors may be universally accepted but perceived differently; ensure measures are meaningful in the specific setting (education availability, community roles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement aim and intended use
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity about whether the instrument is intended to measure resilience as an outcome (e.g., ability to 'bounce back') or as a process/resource inventory, and alignment of instrument properties to that aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select measures according to the intended use: outcome measures need demonstrated responsiveness and MIC; process/resource measures are suited to identifying protective/vulnerability factors to guide interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and respondent burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical suitability of the instrument for the target population, including length, completion time, and likely rates of non-response or missing data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter measures may reduce non-response; pilot testing and qualitative consultation can identify acceptable questionnaire length and format for the population (important for children and different cultural contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and transparency standards for validation studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehensive reporting of psychometric methods and results (test–retest procedures, ICC types, sample sizes, means, SDs, effect sizes, MIC), so others can assess quality and compute sample sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should report as much psychometric information as possible; lack of reporting (e.g., unspecified ICC type, missing sample size details) hampered the review. Present effect sizes or sufficient statistics for meta-analyses and power calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-appropriateness and lifespan generalisability
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the measure is validated for the intended age range (e.g., adults, adolescents, children under 12) and that items are developmentally appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using adult-developed instruments with children/adolescents without validation. The review noted a lack of robust measures for children under 12 and questioned the use of scales developed from older adult samples with younger populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of longitudinal and predictive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of longitudinal studies showing that the measure can predict or reflect resilience outcomes over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longitudinal research can identify key features of resilience and support construct validity; the review used longitudinal evidence to characterise features (family support, external systems, dispositional attitudes). Lack of longitudinal evidence limits inference about change and predictive validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscale validity and coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that identified subscales represent meaningful, theoretically coherent dimensions and that subscale scores behave appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess subscale internal consistency, factor structure, and whether subscales discriminate between groups or predict outcomes. Subscales should align with the overall construct and be interpretable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimising situational/contextual effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Design features and administration procedures that reduce situational influences on responses and improve comparability across settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot and adapt administration protocols to the context; consider school vs. community settings and cultural differences that might influence responses. A good questionnaire seeks to minimise situational effects.
